description: Small concept-curriculum pilot for teaching the material affordance of pouring.
notes: This pilot is general affordance teaching, not benchmark item generation.
The poured material should be central; containers, hands, spouts, and tools should be secondary.
Start with 20 documents so generated quality can be inspected before scaling.
Pour should teach controlled gravity-driven transfer, not only kitchen liquids.
Boundary cases matter: thick pastes may slump, dollop, or need scooping; coarse chunks may tumble or dump; gases usually disperse or flow rather than pour as a central material.

concept_profile.definition: To move a loose or flowing material out of a container or opening, usually downward under gravity, often as a stream, sheet, trickle, or tumbling flow.
concept_profile.centrality_rule: The poured material must be the central participant; the document should not mainly teach about the container, spout, hand, or person.
generation_guidance: Make the target material the thing being poured or failing to pour.
Use containers only as supports for the event; avoid wording that makes the container the main participant.

For positive pour examples, name a source, container, opening, or spout near the first mention of the pouring event, such as a cup, jar, bag, bottle, can, pitcher, bowl, bucket, box, packet, shaker, spout, hole, or opening.
Distinguish controlled pouring from accidental spilling.
For gases and vapors, usually describe them as flowing, dispersing, venting, or filling space rather than being poured as a central material.
For thick or cohesive materials, explain when the material pours, slumps, dollops, scoops, or stays together.

positive_subtypes.label: thin liquids
positive_subtypes.mechanism: thin liquids flow smoothly out of an opening and form a stream under gravity

positive_subtypes.label: viscous liquids
positive_subtypes.mechanism: thick liquids pour slowly because they flow while resisting motion

positive_subtypes.label: powders and grains
positive_subtypes.mechanism: many small loose particles slide past one another and pour like a dry stream

positive_subtypes.label: loose small pieces
positive_subtypes.mechanism: loose pieces can be poured out because the separate pieces tumble and fall together

positive_subtypes.label: slurries and thin mixtures
positive_subtypes.mechanism: liquid and suspended solids move together when the mixture is loose enough to flow

positive_subtypes.label: melted and softened materials
positive_subtypes.mechanism: heating can make some materials fluid enough to pour before they cool and hold shape

negative_subtypes.label: rigid single objects
negative_subtypes.reason: one rigid object can be dropped, placed, or carried, but it does not flow out like a poured material

negative_subtypes.label: cohesive lumps
negative_subtypes.reason: a cohesive lump holds together and may slump, dollop, or need scooping instead of pouring smoothly

negative_subtypes.label: gases and vapors
negative_subtypes.reason: gases spread, vent, flow, or fill space, but they are not usually poured as a visible central material

negative_subtypes.label: fixed structures
negative_subtypes.reason: fixed structures stay attached in place and cannot leave an opening as a poured material

negative_subtypes.label: flexible sheets and fabrics
negative_subtypes.reason: a sheet drapes, folds, or hangs rather than flowing out as a stream

negative_subtypes.label: large mixed objects
negative_subtypes.reason: large objects can be dumped out, but they do not pour with the smooth collective flow of liquid, grains, or small pieces

state_contrasts.lesson: water can be poured as a liquid; a solid ice block must be placed, dropped, or melted before it can pour
melted chocolate can be poured while warm; a solid chocolate bar cannot pour
thin batter can pour; stiff dough usually stretches, folds, or needs scooping
loose sand can pour because grains slide; a packed sand block holds shape until it breaks apart
wet cement can pour when it is loose enough; hardened cement stays rigid

neighbors.label: spill
neighbors.relation: nearby transfer action: spilling is accidental or uncontrolled, while pouring is deliberate and guided

neighbors.label: drip
neighbors.relation: nearby flow pattern: dripping happens in separate drops, while pouring usually forms a stream or larger flow

neighbors.label: dump
neighbors.relation: nearby transfer action: dumping is faster and coarser, often for chunks or many objects

neighbors.label: sprinkle
neighbors.relation: nearby distribution action: sprinkling scatters small amounts over an area instead of sending material out in one main flow

neighbors.label: scoop
neighbors.relation: nearby handling action: scooping lifts material with a tool instead of letting gravity carry it out

neighbors.label: stream
neighbors.relation: nearby outcome: a stream is the flow shape that pouring often creates

neighbors.label: drain
neighbors.relation: nearby transfer action: draining lets material leave through a hole or channel, often without a hand-guided pour

neighbors.label: flow
neighbors.relation: broader behavior: pouring is one controlled way for a material to flow

discourse_styles.description: A plain connective paragraph that places the target concept among nearby material behaviors.
guidance: Connect pouring to a larger family of material behaviors instead of giving only one isolated example.
Name 2-3 nearby actions when natural, such as spill, drip, dump, sprinkle, scoop, stream, drain, or flow.
Explain why the target material fits pouring and why at least one nearby behavior has a different boundary.

discourse_styles.description: Brief, concrete observations of what happens before, during, or after an everyday material event.
guidance: Use plain observed changes instead of abstract labels.
Keep the material behavior visible: flowing, streaming, trickling, tumbling, clumping, slumping, scattering, or staying fixed.

discourse_styles.description: Simple explanatory prose with child-friendly vocabulary and visible causes.
guidance: Use short, clear causal language.
Avoid dense terminology and microscopic mechanisms.

discourse_styles.description: A small ordinary scene where a person uses, prepares, notices, or changes a material.
guidance: Make the scene ordinary and concrete.
Keep the target material central rather than the person, tool, or container.

discourse_styles.description: A compact event sketch that grounds pouring by naming what the material pours from or out of.
guidance: Start near the source frame: the material plus a cup, jar, bag, bottle, pitcher, bowl, bucket, box, packet, shaker, spout, hole, opening, or edge.
Keep the source secondary; the main lesson should still be about how the material pours or fails to pour.
Make the direction of movement visible: out, downward, into another place, onto a surface, or through an opening.

discourse_styles.description: A practical note about how to move, prepare, clean up, or transfer a material.
guidance: Use a practical situation such as cooking, pouring into a mold, filling a jar, cleanup, art, or workshop handling.
Name the material, the source, and the destination when natural.
Mention a nearby alternative action when the material does not pour cleanly, such as scoop, scrape, dump, sprinkle, place, wipe, or let settle.
Keep the prose natural for pretraining, not a recipe checklist.

signal_orders.description: Start with the target affordance, then contrast with a negative or neighbor-winning case.
guidance: Lead with the material that fits the target action.
Then name a material, state, or neighbor action where the target action is not the best description.
Make the contrast explicit without turning the document into a quiz.

signal_orders.description: Start with the negative or neighbor-winning case, then explain the positive target affordance.
guidance: Lead with a material or state where the target action does not fit.
Then introduce the material that does fit the target action.
Use this order to reduce target-word-first bias.

signal_orders.description: Start by naming a nearby action that wins for another material, then contrast with the target action.
guidance: Begin with the neighbor action as the better description for one material.
Then explain why the target action fits the specified target material.
Keep both actions grounded in material behavior.

signal_orders.description: Start with the target action, then name the neighbor action that wins elsewhere.
guidance: Begin with the target action and the specified positive material.
Then name a neighbor action that is better for a different material or state.
Avoid implying the target action is the default for all materials.

signal_orders.description: Present two materials in parallel and assign different actions to each.
guidance: Use a parallel comparison of two materials or states.
Assign the target action to the material that supports it.
Assign a different neighbor action or response to the material that does not support it.
